question: A service method annotated with @Transactional loads a Course with entityManager.find, calls course.rename("Java 25") and returns, without calling any save method. What happens to the database?
options: Nothing, because no save or persist call was made
An UPDATE runs at flush, because the entity is managed and Hibernate detects the changed title
An exception is thrown because the entity was not merged
A new row is inserted with the new title
explanation: Inside the transaction the entity is managed. During flush Hibernate compares it with its load-time snapshot and writes the difference, so no explicit save is needed.

question: A service returns a Course after its @Transactional method ended. The controller then calls course.rename("New title"). Why is the change not stored?
options: The entity is detached, so no persistence context tracks the change
Hibernate caches updates until the next application restart
The title column is marked nullable = false
rename is a method, and only setters are tracked
explanation: When the transaction ends the context closes and the entity becomes detached. Dirty checking only applies to managed entities, so the change must go through a new transaction.

question: A teammate turns the Course entity into a Java record to make it immutable. What is the problem?
options: Records cannot have fields annotated with @Column
Records cannot be serialized
The specification does not allow a record to be an entity, and Hibernate needs a no-argument constructor and mutable state
Records are only allowed with GenerationType.UUID
explanation: Jakarta Persistence forbids records as entities. Records still work well as DTOs and projections, where they only carry query results.

question: A Level enum is stored with the default JPA mapping. Months later someone inserts INTERMEDIATE between BEGINNER and ADVANCED. What is the consequence?
options: Hibernate rewrites the stored numbers automatically
Nothing, because ordinals are fixed once saved
The application fails to start
Stored ordinals now point to different constants, so existing rows change meaning
explanation: The default stores the ordinal, which is a position. Inserting a constant shifts positions. Annotating the field with @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING) stores the name instead.

question: You deploy to a PostgreSQL database that is managed with migration scripts. Which ddl-auto value is the safest to catch a mapping that no longer matches the schema?
options: create-drop
update
validate
create
explanation: validate checks the mappings against the existing schema and fails at startup on a mismatch without changing anything. The other values create or alter objects, or drop the schema.
